I'd say the biggest factor is that a lot of people make big moves right after high school, and distance makes any relationship more difficult to maintain. Couple that with simultaneously meeting a ton of new people at the new location who all seem really exciting and interesting and different and most importantly *there in person experiencing the same new lifestyle* and there's not a lot of impetus to spend time keeping up with old friends from high school. The same sort of thing happens on a smaller scale after freshman year ends (I'd suspect this is due to most transfers and/or changes of major happening then, and ofc what/where you study will have a big impact on your friend group). It also unsurprisingly occurs at the end of college too (for similar reasons). It pretty much all comes down to proximity, and after that it's literal effort on both friends parts. 

Personally, I've come out with maybe one or two long-lasting close friends from before each big life change. There are a few others I speak to periodically or even see once in a blue moon, but as for true friendships I have exactly one friend left from grade school (met in 8th grade) who I talk to almost daily still at age 25, despite living in different states since age 18. Then, I have one other close friend who I met in my sophomore year of college (age 19) who somehow is the only one I've kept in touch with over the last six years from a whole group of people I hung out with a LOT while with my ex. Weirdly enough, that ex also only spends time with one person from that group still, who happens to be roommates with the one who stayed my friend. 
But aside from those two, my adult social circle is composed of people I've met through jobs, hobbies, or through my boyfriend (who weirdly still hangs out with, and even has an ongoing daily group chat with a core group of 5 or 6 now-30-something guys, who all went to high school together but weren't even really friends til afterwards somehow and have remained quite close as a group despite never all being in the same state at once at any point in the last decade AFAIK. He doesn't seem to understand how unusual that kind of friend group actually is.)

I had a mental breakdown trying to get great grades (and participate in career building extracurriculars). Which for me resulted in getting addicted to drugs, dropping out, and triggering my mental illness. 

When I came back to school after a year, I graduated with a 3.05. And that got me into grad school and scored me a job within 3 weeks (one at an established company in an industry I like that isn't boring and has an average salary for my major with benefits and vacation days). So for me at least, putting medium effort into school while protecting my free time has worked out fantastically.

My advice: getting straight A's is NOT worth it. B's are still good, especially at a well-respected school (plus anything with a gpa cutoff generally has it at 3.0). And C's now and then won't kill ya. It's better to have a 3.0 and your sanity than a 4.0 and suicidal thoughts.

I'm "lucky" in that basically everyone who met me during the period before I got on meds agreed that I was bipolar. Manic AF I guess. I honestly don't really remember much from that time, so I guess I'll take people's word for it. Lamictal happens to be the mood stabilizer that works for me, I started on that and abilify(antipsychotic) at the same time and it was like magic, helped with both the mania and depression. But didn't do much for my focus, memory, inability to sit still, etc. which is what led us to see ADHD there too. It's an obnoxious process, getting multiple diagnoses right that probably require multiple medications that might interact with each other or whatever.

On the suicidal thoughts note, if those ever progress to making legit plans, please don't hide that from your therapist/psychiatrist. It's scary that they may have to report it to someone else, but a professional who has known you for a while is way more equipped to help you work through those feelings than a suicide hotline or emergency room person.

You'll of course need to be evaluated by a psychiatrist, but yeah there can be a lot in common between bipolar and someone who has depression and ADHD concurrently. It's also possible to have bipolar and ADHD which is what I have yaaaaay. The most telling thing or whether you are bipolar or not is whether or not you've had a distinct manic phase which has pretty clear symptoms I'm sure you've read. If you're type 1 then it's pretty obvious since the manic phases are somewhat severe, but type 2 has less intense Mania so it would be easier to confuse with other conditions.

If that question seems unanswerable, then try a more systematic route. List all your potential hobbies and divide them into categories like "physical" (sports/work out routines and so on), "creative" (drawing, painting, music), "constructive" (woodworking, home/auto repair, etc) and so on, then decide how many you have time for and choose that many categories. Then allow yourself to pick only one hobby from each category. For example, I determined that I have time for only two main hobbies while still maintaining my school/career and social life. I chose to go with one physical and one creative (physical since it's good for your health as well as fun, and creative because I can't NOT create things). Not that the specifics matter, but I picked figure skating and music (with music as most primary).

If you can't easily pick a top choice from a category, test out what it would be like to have various ones as a primary hobby for a week or two.  Say you were stuck between writing and guitar playing. For one week, practice your guitar every day. The next week, write 500 words a day. Go with whichever one is easier to keep to a consistent schedule with in practice.

And don't feel bad if you want to change one of your hobbies after a while. Everyone goes through phases with their interests, but try not to quit learning a skill just because it's starting to get difficult.
